knitr::opts_chunk$set(message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)

This document is the R Markdown counterpart of the Python notebook
[Part 00 - Introduction](../Notebooks/Part%2000%20-%20Introduction.ipynb).
It performs the same first steps — authenticating, retrieving profiles,
feeds, follows, and followers, and (carefully) writing content — using
[bskyr](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/), an R interface to the
Bluesky API by Christopher Kenny, together with the
[tidyverse](https://www.tidyverse.org/).

## Background

Researchers studying social media spent a decade building methods on
Twitter's APIs; when that access was shut off, attention turned to open
platforms. Bluesky runs on the [AT Protocol](https://atproto.com), an
open protocol whose data is public by design: profiles, posts, follows,
likes, and reposts can all be retrieved through documented endpoints at
[endpoints.bsky.app](https://endpoints.bsky.app). The Python series accesses those
endpoints through the `atproto` SDK; here we use bskyr, which wraps the
same endpoints in R functions that return
[tibbles](https://tibble.tidyverse.org/) ready for tidyverse analysis.

### Learning objectives

By the end of this document you will be able to:

1. Explain what Bluesky and the AT Protocol are, and why bskyr needs an
   account even to read public data.
2. Create an **app password** and store your credentials safely.
3. Retrieve profiles, author feeds, follows, and followers, and read what
   they return: **handles**, **DIDs**, posts, and records.
4. Explain how a **cursor** pages through long lists, and let bskyr follow
   cursors for you.
5. Describe how to write to the network (posts, likes, images with alt
   text), and why these tutorials never do it automatically.
6. Find the right documentation for a question: the API reference, the
   protocol documentation, or the bskyr reference.

### Code

Install the packages once:

```{r install, eval=FALSE}
install.packages(c("bskyr", "tidyverse", "jsonlite"))
```

Then load them. Each plays a distinct role that you will see in every
part of this series: **bskyr** talks to the Bluesky API, the
**tidyverse** (dplyr, ggplot2, purrr, and friends) manipulates and
plots the data that comes back, and **jsonlite** reads and writes JSON,
the format APIs speak:

```{r libraries}
library(bskyr)
library(tidyverse)
library(jsonlite)
```

### Setup

bskyr authenticates with your handle and an **app password**: a separate,
randomly generated password that works only for apps like this one. In the
Bluesky app, go to **Settings → Privacy and security → App passwords**
(or [bsky.app/settings/app-passwords](https://bsky.app/settings/app-passwords)),
add one, and copy it — it's shown only once. An app password can't change
your account's email, password, or security settings, and you can revoke
it at any time. Never put your main account password in code. There are
two ways to supply credentials:

1. Set `BLUESKY_APP_USER` and `BLUESKY_APP_PASS` in your `~/.Renviron`
   (bskyr's native mechanism, via [`bs_set_user()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_set_user.html) and [`bs_set_pass()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_set_pass.html)).
2. Save an `atproto.json` file — the same file the Python notebooks use —
   in the repository root: `{"handle": "you.bsky.social", "password": "..."}`.
   It is gitignored, so credentials never end up in version control.

The shared helper `bsky_client.R` checks both locations and records
whether we are authenticated. **Unlike the Python series, which falls
back to Bluesky's public AppView for read endpoints, bskyr (as of 0.4.x)
sends every request through the authenticated PDS** — so without
credentials the API chunks in this document are skipped when knitting.

## Client

```{r connect}
source("bsky_client.R")
# Without credentials, skip every chunk from here on but keep the prose
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = bsky_authed)
```

When credentials are present, [`bs_auth()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_auth.html) exchanges them for a session
token that every subsequent bskyr call reuses (it is cached for a few
minutes, so repeated calls don't re-authenticate).

## Profile

[`bs_get_profile()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_profile.html) wraps the API endpoint `app.bsky.actor.getProfiles`
and returns one row per requested account.

Two identifiers appear in every profile, and the difference matters for
research. The **handle** (`nytimes.com`) is the human-readable name;
handles are domain names, and an account can change its handle at any
time. The **DID** (Decentralized Identifier, `did:plc:...`) is the
account's permanent, machine-readable ID, which never changes. When you
store data about accounts, key it on DIDs.

Let's look at our own profile first. Two pieces of R syntax to get comfortable with right away: the
pipe `|>` sends the result of one step into the next (read it as
"then"), and `glimpse()` prints a wide tibble sideways so every column
fits on screen:

```{r own-profile}
me <- bs_get_profile(bs_get_user())

me |>
  select(handle, display_name, followers_count, follows_count,
         posts_count, created_at) |>
  glimpse()
```

The numbers you see are live: run this tomorrow and the follower count
may differ. The `description`, `avatar`, and other fields are columns
too — a tibble row plays the role the typed `ProfileView` model plays in
the Python series.

### Retrieving other users' profiles

Any public account can be looked up by handle. `bsky.app` is the
platform's official account:

```{r bsky-profile}
bsky_app <- bs_get_profile("bsky.app")

bsky_app |>
  select(handle, display_name, followers_count, posts_count, created_at)
```

`bs_get_profile()` is vectorized: pass several handles at once and each
becomes a row, which is how Part 01 hydrates accounts in batches.

## Posts

[`bs_get_author_feed()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_author_feed.html) wraps `app.bsky.feed.getAuthorFeed` and returns an
account's recent posts, newest first. Each row is one feed item, and the
post's engagement counters (`like_count`, `repost_count`, ...) are
ordinary columns. The author's actual words live somewhere new: a
**list-column** named `record`, where each cell holds the structured
record the author's client wrote (text, timestamp, languages, facets).
List-columns are how tibbles store nested API data, and
`purrr::map_chr()` is how we reach into them — "for each element of
`record`, pull out `text` as a character string":

```{r author-feed}
profile_feed <- bs_get_author_feed("nytimes.com", limit = 100)

nrow(profile_feed)

profile_feed |>
  mutate(created_at = map_chr(record, "created_at", .default = NA),
         text = map_chr(record, "text", .default = NA)) |>
  select(created_at, text, like_count, repost_count) |>
  head(5)
```

Note where `created_at` comes from: the **record**, which holds what the
author's app wrote, including when the post was written. The tibble also
has an `indexed_at` column, which is when Bluesky's servers *processed*
the post. The two usually agree to within seconds, but they mean
different things, so use the record's timestamp when you mean "when was
this posted".

This `mutate()` + `map_chr()` pattern appears in every part of the
series — it is the single most useful idiom for working with bskyr's
output.

## Where to find documentation

You have now called your first endpoint, so this is a good moment to learn where its documentation lives. There are four sources, and each one answers a *different* question. Most of the time a beginner loses looking something up is spent asking the right question of the wrong source.

| Source | What it is | Published by | The question it answers | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [endpoints.bsky.app](https://endpoints.bsky.app) | The **Bluesky HTTP API reference**: an interactive page for every endpoint | Bluesky Social PBC | *What can I call, with which parameters, and what comes back?* Parameters (including their allowed values), response fields, and which server answers which requests | It doesn't reliably tell you which endpoints need a login: it lists no login requirement for search or the timeline, yet both refuse anonymous callers. When in doubt, try the call, as this series does. |
| [atproto.com](https://atproto.com/docs) | The **AT Protocol** documentation: concepts, guides, and the formal specifications | Bluesky Social PBC | *How does the network work?* Why a DID is permanent and a handle isn't, what a record and a repository are, what the firehose carries | It describes the protocol, not the individual `app.bsky.*` endpoints. |
| [atproto.blue](https://atproto.blue) | Documentation for the **Python `atproto` SDK** this series uses | A community project ([MarshalX/atproto](https://github.com/MarshalX/atproto)), not Bluesky itself | *How do I write this call in Python, and what attributes will the object have?* | The SDK is pre-1.0, and its maintainers warn that compatibility between versions is not guaranteed. That is why this repository pins its version. |
| [bskyr reference](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/) | Documentation for the **R package bskyr**, the R series' counterpart of atproto.blue | Christopher Kenny | *How do I write this call in R, and what columns will the tibble have?* | bskyr logs in for every call, even to read public data. |

### One endpoint, four views

Take the call you just made, which fetched an account's recent posts, and look it up in each source:

1. **Its name.** `app.bsky.feed.getAuthorFeed` is an [NSID](https://atproto.com/specs/nsid) (namespaced identifier): reversed-domain-style dotted words naming a method. The method is defined in a [Lexicon](https://atproto.com/specs/lexicon) schema and called over [XRPC](https://atproto.com/specs/xrpc), the protocol's convention for HTTP requests. Those three terms are atproto.com's territory.
2. **Its contract.** [Its page on endpoints.bsky.app](https://endpoints.bsky.app/#bluesky-app/tag/appbskyfeed/GET/xrpc/app.bsky.feed.getAuthorFeed) lists every parameter and response field. It also shows options this series rarely uses: `filter` values such as `posts_with_video` and `posts_and_author_threads`, and an `includePins` switch. The reference is where you discover what an endpoint *can* do.
3. **In Python** it is `client.get_author_feed(...)`, or equivalently `client.app.bsky.feed.get_author_feed({...})`, documented [on atproto.blue](https://atproto.blue/atproto_client/client/#atproto_client.client.client.Client.get_author_feed).
4. **In R** it is `bs_get_author_feed()`, documented [in the bskyr reference](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_author_feed.html).

A tip for finding an endpoint's page on endpoints.bsky.app: the addresses follow a pattern, `https://endpoints.bsky.app/#bluesky-app/tag/<namespace without the dots>/GET/xrpc/<NSID>`. For `app.bsky.graph.getFollows`, the namespace is `app.bsky.graph`, so the tag is `appbskygraph`. (Two exceptions in this series: the raw firehose, `com.atproto.sync.subscribeRepos`, is documented in the [event-stream specification](https://atproto.com/specs/event-stream) on atproto.com, and Jetstream has its own document on endpoints.bsky.app, which Part 10 links.) The old `docs.bsky.app` site that older tutorials link to has been retired; its endpoint links now land on the reference's front page.

## Timeline

The home timeline — the reverse-chronological feed of accounts *you*
follow — is defined relative to the logged-in account, which is why this
endpoint always requires authentication:

[`bs_get_timeline()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_timeline.html) returns a differently shaped tibble from the other
functions: the author is a packed column (`post_author`, whose `handle`
we reach with `$`), and the record is the list-column `post_record`. To
avoid printing other people's posts, we list only the first few authors:

```{r timeline}
timeline <- bs_get_timeline(limit = 25)

nrow(timeline)
head(timeline$post_author$handle, 5)
```

## Relationships

### Follows

[`bs_get_follows()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_follows.html) wraps `app.bsky.graph.getFollows`: the accounts an
actor follows, one profile per row.

```{r follows}
follows <- bs_get_follows("nytimes.com", limit = 100)

nrow(follows)
follows |> select(did, handle, display_name) |> head(5)
```

These endpoints are *paginated*: each request returns at most 100
records plus a `cursor` — an opaque bookmark marking where the next page
starts. bskyr tucks the cursor away as an *attribute* of the tibble
(metadata attached to the object, read with `attr()`), and —
conveniently — when you ask for `limit > 100` it follows the cursors for
you, making one request per hundred records:

```{r follows-cursor}
attr(follows, "cursor")$cursor

all_follows <- bs_get_follows("nytimes.com", limit = 1000)
nrow(all_follows)
```

If `nrow(all_follows)` came back smaller than 1,000, that is not an
error — it means we reached the end of the list before reaching our
limit. The limit is a *budget*, not a promise.

Part 01 unpacks exactly what is happening under the hood here.

### Followers

[`bs_get_followers()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_followers.html) is the mirror image: accounts that follow the actor.
Followers are mostly private individuals who never chose to be in your
dataset, so rather than printing anyone's profile, we look at what *kind*
of information each row contains:

```{r followers}
followers <- bs_get_followers("nytimes.com", limit = 100)

nrow(followers)
names(followers)
```

Showing the structure instead of a stranger's profile is a habit worth
keeping. You can design an analysis without looking at any individual's
data, and when you do need records, store and report them in aggregate.

## Posting content

Reading is safe to do freely; **writing changes the public record**, so
the chunks below are shown but never executed when this document is knit
(`eval=FALSE`). Run them deliberately, from your own account, when you
mean to.

### Writing a post

```{r post, eval=FALSE}
bs_post(text = "I am posting this from an R Markdown notebook!")
```

### Liking a post

[`bs_like()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_like.html) points at a post by its `uri` (its permanent AT Protocol
address: the author's DID, the record type, and a record key) and its
`cid` (a hash of the post's exact content). Both are columns in any feed
tibble:

```{r like, eval=FALSE}
bs_like(uri = profile_feed$uri[[1]], cid = profile_feed$cid[[1]])
```

### Writing a post with an image

[`bs_post()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_post.html) uploads images for you and attaches alt text — which Part 07
shows is both an accessibility practice and a research object:

```{r post-image, eval=FALSE}
bs_post(
  text = "Now we are sending images from a notebook!",
  images = "my_image.jpg",
  images_alt = "A short description of what the image shows"
)
```

Part 10 builds a bot that posts automatically, along with the disclosure
and rate limits that a bot needs.

## Ethics and limitations

**Public is not the same as consented.** Everything this document reads
is public, but that doesn't mean the people behind it expect to appear
in a dataset. Research on Twitter found that users are often surprised,
and sometimes upset, to learn their posts are used in research (Fiesler &
Proferes 2018). This series studies institutional accounts by default,
prefers aggregates to individual records, and treats ethics as a design
decision made *before* collecting — a theme Part 01 develops in depth.

**Protect your credentials.** An app password can post as you. Keep it in
`atproto.json` or `~/.Renviron` (never in a document), don't share it,
and revoke it if it leaks.

**Limitations.** Everything here is a live snapshot: counts and feeds
change by the minute, posts get deleted, and handles change (DIDs don't).
And Bluesky's users are not "the public": the platform skews toward early
adopters and people who left Twitter.

## Exercises

1. **Another account.** Retrieve the profile of a news organization,
   university, or government agency you're interested in, and compare its
   follower and follow counts with `nytimes.com`'s.
2. **Handles versus DIDs.** Look up `bsky.app` by its DID
   (`bs_get_profile(bsky_app$did)`). Do you get the same profile? Why is
   this useful for research that runs over months?
3. **Reposts in a feed.** How many of the 100 rows in `profile_feed` are
   reposts of someone else's post? (Compare `author_handle` with
   `"nytimes.com"`.)
4. **Budgets versus promises.** Ask `bs_get_follows()` for `limit = 50`,
   `100`, and `1000` for `nytimes.com`. How many rows come back each time,
   and why?
5. **Explore the fields.** Pick a column of `bs_get_profile("nytimes.com")`
   you don't recognize, look it up in the
   [API reference](https://endpoints.bsky.app/#bluesky-app/tag/appbskyactor/GET/xrpc/app.bsky.actor.getProfile),
   and write one sentence on how a researcher might use it.

## Research project ideas

* **Institutional adoption of Bluesky.** Collect the profiles and recent
  posting of a defined population of institutional accounts (for example,
  every newspaper on a public list) and compare how sectors use the
  platform.
* **Audience versus attention.** For a few dozen public institutional
  accounts, plot median likes per post against follower count on log
  scales, and ask whether bigger audiences buy proportionally more
  engagement.
